advance_directive_name: Advance Directive for Health Care (living will and health care proxy combined)
advance_directive_requirements: The form is set out in Ala. Code § 22-8A-4. It must be in writing, signed and dated, and witnessed by two people age 19 or older; no notary is required.
hospice_refusal: An adult age 19 or older who is alert and mentally capable may refuse any medical procedure or treatment, including life-saving and life-sustaining treatment and artificially provided food and liquids. Hospice care focuses on comfort and pain relief, and a person may stop curative treatment.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Alabama. The Assisted Suicide Ban Act, Ala. Code §§ 22-8B-1 to 22-8B-7 (2017), makes it a Class C felony for a physician or health care provider to prescribe a drug or perform a procedure deliberately to aid in dying.
notes: The prohibiting statute cite (Ala. Code §§ 22-8B-1 to 22-8B-7) comes from a secondary summary of the 2017 act; the Alabama Medicaid advance-directive page is the official source for the form.
polst_note: Alabama has no statewide POLST program or statutory POLST form; do-not-resuscitate orders are handled separately by a physician.
proxy_how: Name a competent adult in Part 2 of the Advance Directive for Health Care under Ala. Code § 22-8A-4. The proxy decides on providing, withholding, or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment and artificially provided nutrition and hydration when the person is terminally ill or permanently unconscious, and only as the directive authorizes.
proxy_name: Health care proxy

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive
advance_directive_requirements: Under AS 13.52.010, the directive must be in writing, contain the date of its execution, be signed by the principal, and be witnessed as specified in that section.
hospice_refusal: An adult may give individual instructions, oral or written, refusing treatment under AS 13.52.010, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort. A health care agent or surrogate may make decisions if the person lacks capacity.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Alaska. The only bill considered, HB 54 (2017-2018, the Alaska Voluntary Termination of Life by Terminally Ill Individuals Act), passed one committee and died without becoming law.
notes: No official Alaska page with a downloadable POLST form was returned, so polst_url is null. The toll-free referral number 1-800-770-9999 also appears on the Alaska Bar site but the Anchorage number above was used.
polst_name: POLST (Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: Alaska recognizes a statewide POLST under AS 13.52; since 2022 (HB 392) advanced practice registered nurses and physician assistants may also sign it. The form is completed with a health care provider and does not replace an advance health care directive.
proxy_how: Execute a durable power of attorney for health care under AS 13.52.010(b). The agent may make any health care decision the principal could have made while having capacity, and must follow the principal's instructions and known wishes.
proxy_name: Durable power of attorney for health care (health care agent)

advance_directive_name: Life Care Planning packet (Health Care Power of Attorney and Living Will)
advance_directive_requirements: Sign and date the form in front of at least one adult witness or a notary public under A.R.S. § 36-3221. The witness or notary may not be the agent or a person directly involved in the signer's health care at the time.
hospice_refusal: An adult may refuse medical treatment in a living will or through a health care agent, including life-sustaining treatment when terminally ill or permanently unconscious. Hospice care provides comfort care, and a person may decline curative treatment.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Arizona. Assisting a suicide is treated as manslaughter under A.R.S. § 13-1103, with no exception for physicians or terminal illness.
notes: The State Bar of Arizona does not run a traditional phone lawyer-referral service; its public page links to Find-a-Lawyer and low-cost programs, so no referral phone is listed.
polst_name: POLST (Portable Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: A POLST is a provider-signed medical order for a person who is seriously ill or frail. A blank POLST form is available through the Attorney General's Life Care Planning materials, and it is completed with a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in the Health Care Power of Attorney form (A.R.S. §§ 36-3221 et seq.). The agent makes health care decisions, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, when the person cannot make or communicate them.
proxy_name: Health care agent (Health Care Power of Attorney)

advance_directive_name: Advance Care Plan Form and Appointment of Health Care Agent Form
advance_directive_requirements: A written advance directive must be either notarized or witnessed by two competent adult witnesses under the Arkansas Health Care Decisions Act.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may state in a declaration (living will) whether life-sustaining treatment should be withheld or withdrawn if terminally ill or permanently unconscious, once two physicians make that determination. Hospice care focuses on comfort, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Arkansas. A bill to authorize it, HB 1536 (the Compassionate Care End-of-Life Option Act, 2019), died in committee and was never enacted.
notes: No specific Arkansas statute criminalizing assisted suicide was verified from an official source, so maid_law is null. The living will is governed by the Arkansas Rights of the Terminally Ill or Permanently Unconscious Act.
polst_name: AR POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: The Arkansas Department of Health prescribes the standardized pink POLST form under Act 504 of 2017. It is signed by the patient's physician and by the patient or legal representative, and it complements but does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent using the Appointment of Health Care Agent Form from the Arkansas Department of Health. The agent makes health care decisions for the person when the person lacks capacity, following the person's instructions and wishes.
proxy_name: Health care agent

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop any medical treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort and pain relief. An advance health care directive or agent carries out those wishes if the person cannot communicate.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older with capacity to make medical decisions who has a terminal disease, meaning an incurable and irreversible disease that will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months.
maid_law: California End of Life Option Act, Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 443-443.22
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests to the attending physician at least 48 hours apart and one written request, confirmed by a consulting physician. Only the person may make the request and self-administer the drug; no one may request it on their behalf, including through an advance directive, and the person may rescind at any time.
notes: SB 380 shortened the oral-request interval to 48 hours (eff. Jan 1, 2022); the Jan 1, 2031 sunset was repealed by SB 403 (signed Oct 3, 2025) and the Act now continues indefinitely. Advance directive form is the statutory form (Probate Code § 4701) from the Attorney General; witness requirements not verified, so that field stays null.
polst_name: POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: POLST is a standardized, immediately actionable physician order under Cal. Prob. Code §§ 4780-4785 for a person who is frail or elderly, has a compromised condition, or has a terminal illness. It supplements but does not replace an advance health care directive, and the official form is available at capolst.org.
proxy_how: Name an agent in an Advance Health Care Directive under Cal. Prob. Code Division 4.7. The agent makes health care decisions when the person is unable to make or communicate them, following the person's instructions and wishes.
proxy_name: Health care agent (agent under an Advance Health Care Directive)

advance_directive_name: Medical Durable Power of Attorney (MDPOA) and living will (declaration as to medical treatment)
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop medical treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, through an advance directive or agent. Hospice care provides comfort-focused care, and a person may decline curative treatment.
maid_eligibility: An adult resident of Colorado age 18 or older who is mentally capable, can make and communicate an informed decision, and has a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less, confirmed by two physicians.
maid_law: Colorado End-of-Life Options Act, C.R.S. §§ 25-48-101 to 25-48-123 (enacted by Proposition 106, 2016)
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request witnessed by two people. Either physician must refer the person for a mental-health evaluation if capability is in doubt, and the person may rescind the request at any time and may choose not to use the medication.
notes: Colorado has no statewide lawyer-referral service; the Colorado Bar Association page states it does not make individual referrals and directs the public to its Find-a-Lawyer directory, so help_phone is null. Witness requirements for the MDPOA were not verified from an official source, so that field is null.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: MOST is Colorado's version of POLST: a medical order for a seriously ill person that records preferences for CPR, artificial nutrition and hydration, and other life-sustaining treatments. It is completed with a health care provider and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Complete a Medical Durable Power of Attorney under C.R.S. §§ 15-14-503 to 15-14-509 naming a health care agent. The agent makes medical decisions for the person if the person becomes unable to speak for them. In Colorado no one, including a spouse or adult child, can automatically make medical decisions for another adult.
proxy_name: Health care agent (named in a Medical Durable Power of Attorney)

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (living will and appointment of health care representative, combined form available)
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be signed by the declarant and witnessed by two witnesses; a notary public may also witness it, and an optional witnesses' affidavit is available. No lawyer is needed to complete the forms.
hospice_refusal: MOLST and the living will rest on the right to accept or refuse medical treatment, including treatments that might extend life. A person may refuse or stop treatment and choose hospice care focused on comfort.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Connecticut. Connecticut has no aid-in-dying law, and bills to create one have been introduced but not enacted.
notes: Connecticut has no statewide lawyer-referral service; referrals are handled by county bar associations, so no statewide referral phone is listed. No specific Connecticut statute criminalizing assisted suicide was verified from an official source, so maid_law is null.
polst_name: MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: MOLST is a medical order authorized statewide by Public Act 17-70 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-580h) for a person approaching the end stage of a serious, life-limiting illness or in advanced chronic progressive frailty. It is voluntary, is not an advance directive, and is completed with a clinician.
proxy_how: Appoint a health care representative in writing under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-575a. The representative may make any and all health care decisions on the person's behalf, including whether to withhold or withdraw life support, when the person is unable to make or communicate decisions.
proxy_name: Health care representative

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (health-care instruction and power of attorney for health care)
advance_directive_requirements: Under the rewritten 16 Del. C. ch. 25, a health-care instruction requires no signature, witness, or writing, while a power of attorney for health care must be a signed record witnessed by one adult witness.
hospice_refusal: An adult with decision-making capacity may plan ahead through an advance health care directive or a DMOST form and have those wishes respected, including refusing life-sustaining treatment. Hospice care provides comfort care, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_eligibility: An adult resident of Delaware with a terminal illness and a prognosis of six months or less to live, who has decision-making capacity, is making an informed decision, and is acting voluntarily, as confirmed by both an attending physician or APRN and a consulting physician or APRN.
maid_law: The Ron Silverio/Heather Block End of Life Options Law, 16 Del. C. ch. 25C (House Bill 140, signed May 20, 2025; in effect January 1, 2026)
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests and one written request; the second oral request must come at least 15 days after the first, and the written request must be signed by two adult witnesses. Only the person may request the medication, not a guardian, surrogate, or agent, and the person may rescind at any time. Providers must report prescriptions to the Department of Health and Social Services. No prescription may be filled less than 48 hours after the written request.
notes: Final regulations published by the Register of Regulations on March 1. A 2026 bill (SB 274) proposes renaming DMOST to POLST. Advance-directive chapter rewritten (84 Del. Laws ch. 467), effective Sept 30, 2025: a health-care instruction needs no signature, witness, or writing; a power of attorney for health care must be a signed record witnessed by one adult witness.
polst_name: DMOST (Delaware Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: DMOST is a portable medical order under 16 Del. C. ch. 25A for a patient with serious illness or frailty whose practitioner would not be surprised if they died within the next year. It must be signed by the patient or authorized representative and a physician, APRN, or physician assistant, and it is separate from an advance health care directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in a power of attorney for health care under 16 Del. C. § 2508. The agent makes health care decisions when the person is found to lack capacity, following the person's instructions and wishes.
proxy_name: Agent (under a power of attorney for health care)

advance_directive_name: Living Will
advance_directive_requirements: Under Fla. Stat. § 765.302, a living will must be signed by the principal in the presence of two subscribing witnesses, one of whom is neither a spouse nor a blood relative of the principal.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may direct in a living will that life-prolonging procedures be withheld or withdrawn if terminally ill, in an end-stage condition, or in a persistent vegetative state, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort and pain relief.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Florida. Fla. Stat. § 782.08 makes deliberately assisting another person's self-murder manslaughter, a second-degree felony punishable by up to 15 years in prison, with no exception for physicians or terminal illness. Fla. Stat. § 765.309 states that the advance-directives chapter does not authorize mercy killing or euthanasia.
notes: A 2025 bill (SB 1700, Florida End-of-Life Options Act) and a prefiled 2026 bill (SB 312) would have authorized aid in dying but were not enacted.
polst_name: POLST — no statewide statutory form; DNRO (Do Not Resuscitate Order, DH Form 1896) used instead
polst_note: Florida has no statewide POLST form in statute. The Department of Health's DNRO (DH Form 1896) is a one-page order, printed on yellow paper and signed by the patient's physician or other authorized provider, directing paramedics and EMTs not to resuscitate. POLST-type orders may also be used in hospitals, facilities, and hospice.
proxy_how: Designate a competent adult as health care surrogate in writing under Fla. Stat. § 765.202. The surrogate makes health care decisions and receives health information needed for those decisions when the principal is incapacitated.
proxy_name: Health care surrogate

advance_directive_name: Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care
advance_directive_requirements: The person must be 18 or older or an emancipated minor and of sound mind, and must sign the form with two witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A person may use the Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care to accept or refuse life-sustaining procedures and artificial nutrition or hydration when terminally ill or permanently unconscious, once the condition is certified in writing. Hospice care provides comfort care, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Georgia. O.C.G.A. § 16-5-5 makes it a felony, punishable by 1 to 10 years in prison, for a person with actual knowledge that someone intends suicide to knowingly and willfully assist in that suicide. The statute does not apply to pain-relief care or to withholding or withdrawing treatment under an advance directive.
notes: The Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care (O.C.G.A. Title 31, Chapter 32) replaced the separate living will and durable power of attorney for health care on July 1, 2007. The State Bar of Georgia states it cannot refer an attorney and directs people to local and voluntary bar associations, so no referral phone is listed.
polst_name: POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: Georgia's POLST is a medical order under O.C.G.A. § 31-1-14 for a patient with a serious illness who is expected to die within 365 days, or with dementia or another progressive degenerative brain condition. It is completed with the attending physician and signed by the patient or an authorized person and the physician.
proxy_how: Name a health care agent in Part 1 of the Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care under O.C.G.A. § 31-32-8. The agent carries out the person's health care decisions when the person cannot, but may not consent to psychosurgery, sterilization, or involuntary hospitalization or treatment.
proxy_name: Health care agent

advance_directive_name: Hawai'i Advance Health Care Directive
advance_directive_requirements: Sign and date the form, and have it signed by two qualified adult witnesses or acknowledged before a notary public. Electronic signatures are not accepted.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse treatment and may choose hospice or palliative care, and the Department of Health encourages patients to explore hospice and palliative care. An advance directive states the person's instructions if they later cannot make decisions.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is a Hawaii resident, has a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less, is competent to make informed health care decisions, and is able to self-administer the medication.
maid_law: Our Care, Our Choice Act, Hawaii Revised Statutes chapter 327L, effective January 1, 2019.
maid_safeguards: The patient must consult three providers (attending, consulting, and a mental-health counseling provider), make two oral requests at least five days apart and one written request signed before two witnesses, and wait at least 48 hours after the written request before a prescription is made available. The patient may rescind at any time, and no provider is required to participate.
notes: As of June 1, 2023, qualified Advanced Practice Registered Nurses may serve as attending or consulting providers. The written-request waiting period is five days under the current law, reduced from the original twenty days.
polst_name: POLST (Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: POLST is a set of medical orders for people with serious illness or advanced frailty, completed with a clinician, and it is different from an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in Part 1 of the Advance Health Care Directive. The agent's authority takes effect when the primary physician determines the person is unable to make health care decisions, unless the form says it takes effect immediately, and the agent may make health care decisions as stated in the form.
proxy_name: Health care agent (durable power of attorney for health care)

advance_directive_name: Idaho Advance Health Care Directive (Living Will and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care)
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be signed by the person making it. It does not need to be notarized or signed by a medical provider.
hospice_refusal: A competent patient, a patient's advance directive, or a surrogate decision-maker may direct that life-sustaining care be withheld or withdrawn, and comfort care must be provided. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Idaho. Idaho Code section 39-4514(2) states the Medical Consent and Natural Death Act does not make legal euthanasia, mercy killing, or assisted suicide, and Idaho Code section 18-4017 makes assisting a suicide a felony.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: POST contains medical orders for a person with a serious illness or approaching end of life and complements an advance directive. It must be completed and signed by the person and a health care provider, and is available through the Idaho Healthcare Directive Registry.
proxy_how: Name an agent in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care part of the Advance Health Care Directive. The agent makes health care decisions when the person cannot communicate or make decisions.
proxy_name: Agent under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Living Will Declaration and Illinois Statutory Short Form Power of Attorney for Health Care
hospice_refusal: A person has the right to refuse medical treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and a living will applies when the person has a terminal condition and cannot state their wishes. The aid-in-dying law requires the physician to inform the patient of all feasible end-of-life options, including hospice and palliative care.
maid_eligibility: An adult Illinois resident with a terminal illness expected to cause death within six months, who has the mental capacity to make medical decisions and is able to self-administer the medication.
maid_law: End-of-Life Options for Terminally Ill Patients Act, 410 ILCS 22 (P.A. 104-0441, also called Deb's Law), signed December 12, 2025, effective September 12, 2026.
maid_safeguards: The attending physician and a consulting physician must both confirm the terminal illness, prognosis, and mental capacity, and the patient must make two oral requests at least five days apart and one written request signed before two witnesses. The waiting period is waived if the patient is expected to die within five days, the patient may rescind at any time, and no physician, provider, or pharmacist is required to participate.
notes: No statewide injunction; the law is in effect statewide. In Payne v. Pritzker the federal court declined a preliminary injunction; TROs in two religious-liberty cases bar enforcement only against those plaintiffs. The signing requirements for the Illinois living will and power of attorney forms were not verified from an official page, so that field is null.
polst_name: POLST (Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment), also called the Uniform Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) Advance Directive
polst_note: A POLST records orders about CPR and life-sustaining treatment and must be signed by the patient or authorized legal representative and the attending practitioner. It is intended to be honored in hospitals, nursing homes, and by emergency medical services.
proxy_how: Name an agent using the Illinois Statutory Short Form Power of Attorney for Health Care. The agent makes health care decisions when a physician determines the person cannot make them, including decisions to accept, withdraw, or decline life-sustaining treatment, unless the form limits that authority.
proxy_name: Health care agent (Health Care Power of Attorney)

advance_directive_name: Health Care Advance Directive (Indiana Code 16-36-7)
advance_directive_requirements: The advance directive must be signed by the person making it and by two witnesses or a notary public. There is no official or mandatory state form, but the document must meet Indiana law to be valid.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may state in an advance directive that life-prolonging procedures be withheld or withdrawn if they have an incurable injury, disease, or illness and death will occur within a short time. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Indiana. Indiana Code section 35-42-1-2.5 makes it a crime for a health care professional to knowingly administer, prescribe, or dispense medications or procedures intended to cause death. The 2026 End of Life Options Act (HB 1011) died in committee.
notes: The Indiana State Bar Association states it does not provide legal advice or referrals itself; its Get Legal Help page directs people to Indiana Legal Help and to its Locate Your Lawyer directory.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: POST is for a person with advanced chronic progressive disease, frailty, or a terminal condition. It turns current treatment preferences into medical orders and must be signed by the patient or legal representative and a physician, advanced practice registered nurse, or physician assistant.
proxy_how: Name a health care representative in the advance directive. The representative must be age 18 or older and makes health care decisions when the person cannot make or communicate them.
proxy_name: Health care representative (HCR)

advance_directive_name: Declaration Relating to Use of Life-Sustaining Procedures (Living Will) and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care Decisions
advance_directive_requirements: The document must be signed or acknowledged before a notary public or two witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may execute a declaration directing that life-sustaining procedures be withheld or withdrawn if their condition is terminal and they cannot make treatment decisions. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Iowa. Bills to allow it, including the 2026 Our Care, Our Options Act (HF 2262), died in committee without a hearing.
notes: The Iowa State Bar Association states the public should not call its office seeking referrals; it directs people to the Iowa Find-A-Lawyer website, so no help phone is given here.
polst_name: IPOST (Iowa Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: IPOST is a one-page uniform medical order for a person who is frail or elderly or has a chronic, critical, or terminal condition. It covers resuscitation, scope of treatment, and artificial nutrition, and must be signed by the patient or legal representative and a physician, advanced registered nurse practitioner, or physician assistant.
proxy_how: Name an attorney-in-fact in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care. The agent's authority takes effect when the attending physician or physician assistant determines the person is unable to make health care decisions, and the agent may consent to, refuse, or withdraw consent to care, treatment, or procedures.
proxy_name: Attorney-in-fact (agent) under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Declaration (Living Will) under the Kansas Natural Death Act and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care Decisions
advance_directive_requirements: The declaration and the durable power of attorney must be in writing, signed, and dated, and either signed in the presence of two witnesses age 18 or older or acknowledged before a notary public. A witness may not be the agent, a relative by blood, marriage, or adoption, a person entitled to part of the estate, or a person directly financially responsible for the person's health care.
hospice_refusal: Under the Kansas Natural Death Act, an adult has the right to control decisions about their own medical care, including withholding life-sustaining treatment in a terminal condition certified by two physicians. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Kansas. Bills to allow it, including the Kansas Death With Dignity Act (HB 2202) in the 2021-2022 session, died in committee without a hearing.
notes: Kansas has no statutory default surrogate list; without a signed document, no relative has statutory authority to make health care decisions and the fallback is a district court. The TPOPP form itself is obtained from a clinician through the Center for Practical Bioethics program; the KDHE page above is the official state advance-care-planning page.
polst_name: TPOPP (Transportable Physician Orders for Patient Preferences)
polst_note: TPOPP is a voluntary physician order set, usually for a person with advanced illness, that records current treatment preferences as medical orders. It must be reviewed and signed by a physician to be valid and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care Decisions. The agent may consent to, refuse, or withdraw consent to care, treatment, services, or procedures, and may make decisions about physicians and long-term care, but may not revoke a prior living will declaration.
proxy_name: Agent under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care Decisions

advance_directive_name: Living Will Directive
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be in writing, dated, and signed by the grantor, and either witnessed by two or more adults in the presence of the grantor and each other or acknowledged before a notary public.
hospice_refusal: Under the Kentucky Living Will Directive Act, a person may direct that life-prolonging treatment be withheld or withdrawn and that they be permitted to die naturally with only care needed to relieve pain. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Kentucky. Kentucky Revised Statutes sections 216.302 and 216.308 provide that a health care professional convicted of assisted suicide may have their license revoked. The 2026 bill HB 408 died in committee.
notes: The Kentucky Bar Association page lists local lawyer referral services rather than operating one itself; the phone given is the Kentucky Bar Association number listed by the Attorney General for its Lawyer Referral Service.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: MOST is a voluntary medical order, usually for a person with advanced illness, that records current treatment wishes. It must be reviewed at least annually and is completed by a physician in communication with the patient, surrogate, or responsible party.
proxy_how: Designate one or more health care surrogates in the first section of the Living Will Directive. The surrogate makes health care decisions when the person no longer has decisional capacity, following the wishes stated in the directive.
proxy_name: Health care surrogate

advance_directive_name: Declaration Concerning Life-Sustaining Procedures (Living Will Declaration)
advance_directive_requirements: The written declaration must be signed by the declarant in the presence of two witnesses. It may be registered with the Louisiana Secretary of State.
hospice_refusal: Louisiana law recognizes a person's right to control decisions about their own medical care, including having life-sustaining procedures withheld or withdrawn when diagnosed with a terminal and irreversible condition. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Louisiana. Louisiana legislators have never considered an aid-in-dying bill.
notes: The statewide LaPOST electronic registry was disabled indefinitely as of June 29, 2024. No single statewide LSBA referral phone was verified on an official page, so no help phone is given; the LSBA page lists local bar referral programs.
polst_name: LaPOST (Louisiana Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: LaPOST is a portable physician order for a person with a life-limiting and irreversible condition, covering CPR, medical interventions, and artificially administered nutrition. It must be signed by a physician and the patient or personal health care representative, is voluntary, and complements rather than replaces an advance directive.
proxy_how: A declaration may designate another person to make the treatment decision, and a health care mandate (power of attorney) names an agent to make medical decisions when the person cannot. Louisiana law requires express authority for an agent to make health care decisions.
proxy_name: Personal health care representative (agent under a health care mandate / health care power of attorney)

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be signed by the person making it and by two witnesses. No notary is required.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse treatment, and an advance directive or health care agent states the person's wishes if they later cannot make decisions. The aid-in-dying law requires the physician to discuss alternatives, including palliative care and hospice.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is a Maine resident, is competent, has a terminal disease expected to cause death within six months, and is able to self-administer the medication. A person does not qualify solely because of age or disability.
maid_law: Maine Death with Dignity Act, 22 Maine Revised Statutes chapter 418, section 2140 (Public Law 2019, chapter 271, signed June 12, 2019).
maid_safeguards: The attending physician and a consulting physician must confirm the terminal disease and prognosis, and the patient must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request signed before two witnesses, with at least 48 hours between the written request and the prescription. A 2025 amendment lets the attending physician waive up to 10 days of the waiting period, and the patient may rescind at any time.
notes: The Maine State Bar Association Lawyer Referral Service now accepts requests only through its online form and states it does not accept phone calls for referrals, so no help phone is given. The 2025 waiting-period amendment is Public Law 2025, chapter 375.
polst_name: POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: POLST is an actionable medical order for a person facing a terminal illness or in an advanced state of medical frailty, completed with a clinician, and it is not intended for general use among older adults. advance_directive_name: Maryland Advance Directive: Planning for Future Health Care Decisions
advance_directive_requirements: A written advance directive must be dated, signed, and witnessed by two witnesses. The health care agent may not serve as a witness, at least one witness must not be entitled to any part of the person's estate or otherwise benefit financially from their death, and notarization is not required.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or direct the withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining procedures in an advance directive when death from a terminal condition is imminent or the person is in a persistent vegetative state or an end-stage condition. Hospice care is a comfort-care option for a person with a terminal condition.

polst_name: MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: MOLST is a portable and enduring medical order form covering CPR and other life-sustaining treatments, valid in all health care settings. It must be completed and signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant, and the form is available at marylandmolst.org.

advance_directive_name: Massachusetts Health Care Proxy
advance_directive_requirements: Massachusetts has no living-will statute; the health care proxy under MGL c. 201D is the only advance directive authorized by statute. It must be signed in front of two adult witnesses, who also sign; the named agent cannot be a witness, and no notary is required.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may accept or refuse any health care, including life-prolonging treatment, nutrition and hydration, and may receive palliative care and hospice care. A health care agent may refuse treatment on the person's behalf once capacity is lost.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Massachusetts. MGL c. 201D, § 12 states nothing in that chapter shall be construed to constitute, condone, authorize, or approve suicide or mercy killing. The End of Life Options Act (S. 1486, 2025-2026) is a pending bill and is not law.

polst_name: MOLST (Massachusetts Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)

advance_directive_name: Michigan Advance Directive (Patient Advocate Designation)
advance_directive_requirements: Michigan has no living-will statute; the operative document is the Patient Advocate Designation under MCL 700.5506 et seq. It must be signed in front of two witnesses, and the named patient advocate must sign an acceptance before acting. No notary is required.

maid_prohibited_note: Michigan has no medical aid in dying law. Under MCL 750.329a, knowingly assisting another person to end their life is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000, or both. Senate Bill 681 (2023), the proposed Michigan Death with Dignity Act, stalled in committee and did not become law.
notes: No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services also offers a separate advance directive for mental health care.
polst_name: MI-POST (Michigan Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: MI-POST is an optional medical order for adults with advanced illness or frailty, created by Public Act 154 of 2017. It records decisions about CPR, critical care, and end-of-life goals, is signed by the patient or representative and a clinician, and does not replace an advance directive.

advance_directive_name: Minnesota Health Care Directive
advance_directive_requirements: Under Minn. Stat. § 145C.03, a health care directive must be in writing, dated, and signed, and the signature must be verified by a notary public or by two witnesses. The health care agent cannot act as a witness or notary for the directive.
hospice_refusal: A person may give health care instructions refusing treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and providers must honor those wishes or transfer the person to a provider who will. Hospice and palliative care are available as comfort-focused care for serious illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Minnesota has no medical aid in dying law. Minn. Stat. § 609.215 prohibits aiding suicide, and Minn. Stat. ch. 145C states that no health care directive may override that prohibition. The End-of-Life Option Act (HF 1930 in 2023-2024; SF 3215 / HF 2998 in 2025-2026) did not advance out of committee.

polst_name: POLST (Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: Minnesota POLST is a provider's medical order, signed by a health care provider, that tells first responders what treatments a seriously ill person wants in an emergency. It works alongside a health care directive and does not replace it.

advance_directive_name: Mississippi Advance Health-Care Directive
advance_directive_requirements: Under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 41-41-201 to 41-41-229, with the optional form at § 41-41-209, the directive must be signed by two qualified adult witnesses who know the person, or acknowledged before a notary public in Mississippi. A witness cannot be the agent, a health care provider, or an employee of a health care provider or facility.
hospice_refusal: A person may give instructions to provide, withhold, or withdraw treatment to keep them alive, including artificial nutrition and hydration, and may direct that pain relief be provided at all times even if it hastens death. Hospice care is available as comfort-focused care for terminal illness.

advance_directive_name: Missouri Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Health Care Directive (living will declaration)
advance_directive_requirements: The Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care under RSMo §§ 404.800 to 404.872 must be acknowledged before a notary public. The living will declaration under RSMo §§ 459.010 to 459.055, with a sample form at § 459.015, must be signed in front of two adult witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop treatment, including death-prolonging procedures, through a health care directive. Missouri's living will statute excludes nutrition and hydration from the death-prolonging procedures that can be refused under that statute. Hospice care is available as comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Missouri has no medical aid in dying law, and no authorizing statute was found. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.

polst_name: TPOPP (Transportable Physician Orders for Patient Preferences)
polst_note: Missouri uses TPOPP, a transportable medical order completed with a clinician that records CPR, medical intervention, antibiotic, and nutrition preferences. It does not replace an advance directive, and no official statewide form URL was verified in this research.

advance_directive_name: Montana My Choices Advance Directive (declaration under the Montana Rights of the Terminally Ill Act)
advance_directive_requirements: Under the Montana Rights of the Terminally Ill Act, MCA Title 50, ch. 9, a directive must be signed by a person at least 18 years old and witnessed by two witnesses. Notarization is not required.
hospice_refusal: A person may direct a physician to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment for an incurable or irreversible condition through a declaration under the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act. Hospice and comfort care are available as end-of-life options.
maid_eligibility: A terminally ill, mentally competent adult patient may request physician aid in dying, and the patient must self-administer the prescribed medication. There is no statute setting out who qualifies; eligibility comes only from the court's decision.

maid_safeguards: There are no statutory safeguards, steps, or reporting rules, because Montana has no medical aid in dying statute. The court held only that a terminally ill patient's consent is a defense to a homicide charge against the aiding physician under Montana's consent statute.

A 2025 bill to remove patient consent as a defense (SB 136) was rejected by the House. Montana also has an End-of-Life Registry run by the Attorney General under MCA § 50-9-501.

advance_directive_name: Nevada Advance Directive (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Declaration / living will)

advance_directive_requirements: The Health Care Proxy must be signed in front of two witnesses. New York has no statute governing living wills; a living will is recognized under case law (In re Westchester County Medical Center, 72 N.Y.2d 517 (1988)).

The request may only be made by the patient (not by a health care agent or through an advance directive), and only the patient may self-administer the medication; lethal injection and lethal infusion do not qualify.

advance_directive_name: Oregon Advance Directive for Health Care (OHA 3905)
advance_directive_requirements: You must sign the form, and it must be witnessed by two witnesses or a notary.
hospice_refusal: An advance directive lets you write down treatments you do or do not want, such as a breathing machine or feeding tube, before you need them. You may refuse or withdraw life-sustaining treatment, and a POLST turns those wishes into medical orders.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older who is capable of making and communicating health care decisions and has a terminal illness expected to cause death within six months. The residency requirement was repealed in 2023 (HB 2279).
maid_law: Oregon Death with Dignity Act, ORS 127.800-127.897
maid_safeguards: The patient must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request signed and dated in the presence of two witnesses. An attending physician and a consulting physician must confirm the diagnosis and capacity, the patient may rescind the request at any time, and only the patient may self-administer the medication. Lethal injection, mercy killing, and euthanasia are prohibited.
notes: The 15-day waiting period may be waived for a patient whose death is imminent under the 2019 amendments. The Oregon Health Authority FAQ confirms the POLST registry URL and that POLST forms come from the patient's physician.
polst_name: POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: A POLST is a medical order signed by a physician, naturopathic physician, nurse practitioner, or physician associate, and it is filed in the statewide Oregon POLST Registry (ORS 127.663-127.684). It records wishes for emergency treatment, including resuscitation, and is for seriously ill patients rather than healthy adults.
proxy_how: Name a health care representative in the Advance Directive form. The representative makes health care decisions for you if you become too sick to speak for yourself or are unable to make your own medical decisions. If you have no effective appointment, a representative is appointed for you in the priority order in ORS 127.635.
proxy_name: Health care representative

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (combined Living Will and Durable Health Care Power of Attorney), Act 169 of 2006, 20 Pa.C.S. Chapter 54
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be dated and signed by the principal and two adult witnesses. Notarization is not required in Pennsylvania, but is recommended.
hospice_refusal: A living will takes effect when your attending physician determines you lack the ability to understand, make, or communicate health care decisions and you are permanently unconscious or have an end-stage medical condition. You may refuse or withdraw life-sustaining treatment under the Advance Directive for Health Care Act.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. Under 18 Pa.C.S. 2505, a person who intentionally aids or solicits another to die by suicide is guilty of a felony of the second degree if the conduct causes a suicide or attempted suicide, and otherwise of a misdemeanor of the second degree. Bills to authorize it (HB 1109 / SB 570, 2025) had not passed as of 2026.
notes: The POLST URL is the PA POLST program's official guidance document; the form itself is available through papolst.org. The PBA Lawyer Referral Service covers 47 of 67 counties; other counties use local bar referral services.
polst_name: PA POLST (Pennsylvania Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: PA POLST is a medical order, not an advance directive, for people with serious illness. It is completed by a doctor, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner with the patient, printed on pink card stock, and translates wishes into orders for CPR, medical interventions, and other treatment.
proxy_how: Appoint an agent in the Durable Health Care Power of Attorney part of the Advance Health Care Directive. The agent makes health and personal care decisions for you when you are unable to do so, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, artificial nutrition and hydration, and organ donation.
proxy_name: Health care agent under a Durable Health Care Power of Attorney

advance_directive_name: Living Will Declaration (Rights of the Terminally Ill Act, R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 23-4.11) and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care (Chapter 23-4.10)
advance_directive_requirements: The Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care must be signed by one notary public or two qualified witnesses present when you sign or acknowledge your signature. The living will declaration must be signed in the presence of two subscribing witnesses who are not related to you by blood or marriage.
hospice_refusal: The Rights of the Terminally Ill Act allows a person to instruct physicians to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining procedures in a terminal condition. A competent adult may refuse treatment, and hospice care provides comfort care for a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Rhode Island; no statute authorizes a physician to prescribe medication for that purpose.
notes: Rhode Island does not use the terms health care proxy or health care representative in its statutes; the decision maker is the agent under the durable power of attorney. No specific assisted-suicide prohibition statute was verified from an official source, so that cite is omitted rather than guessed.
polst_name: MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: MOLST, under R.I. Gen. Laws Chapter 23-4.11, is a voluntary medical order signed by the patient or health care decision maker and a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant. It directs providers on resuscitation and life-sustaining measures and travels with the patient between facilities.
proxy_how: Name one agent in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care form. The agent may make any health care decision you could make yourself when your doctor determines you are unable to communicate health care decisions, and no terminal condition is needed for the power to take effect.
proxy_name: Agent (attorney in fact) under a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care

advance_directive_name: Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (living will, S.C. Code Title 44, Chapter 77) and Health Care Power of Attorney (S.C. Code 62-5-501 to 62-5-518)
advance_directive_requirements: The Health Care Power of Attorney must be signed by two witnesses. The Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death must be signed by two witnesses and an officer authorized to administer oaths.
hospice_refusal: Under S.C. Code 44-77-30, life-sustaining procedures may be withheld or withdrawn when a person age 18 or older has a qualifying declaration and two physicians who personally examined the person certify a terminal condition or permanent unconsciousness. Hospice care provides comfort care for a terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized. S.C. Code 16-3-1090 makes it unlawful to assist another person in committing suicide, punishable as a felony by up to 15 years imprisonment or a fine up to $100,000, or both. Note: South Carolina's living-will law is titled the Death With Dignity Act, but it is a declaration for a natural death, not a medical aid in dying law.
notes: South Carolina's living-will statute is titled the Death With Dignity Act (Title 44, Chapter 77), which is a declaration for a natural death, not a medical aid in dying law. The SC Bar page lists the statutory health care power of attorney forms; the POST URL is the official Code chapter text. The statewide toll-free referral number 1-800-868-2284 also appears in state sources, but the SC Bar page itself lists (803) 799-7100, which is used here.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: POST, under the Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment Act (S.C. Code Title 44, Chapter 80, 2019 Act No. 89), is a uniform set of medical orders signed by a patient's physician for a person with a serious illness or who may be expected to lose capacity within twelve months. It is portable across health care settings and covers resuscitation, medical interventions, and assisted nutrition and hydration.
proxy_how: Name an agent age 18 or older and of sound mind in the statutory Health Care Power of Attorney form (S.C. Code 62-5-504); the agent may not be your doctor or another health care provider treating you, or their employee. The agent has full authority to make health care decisions for you when you cannot, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, access to medical records, and placement in a health care or nursing facility.

advance_directive_name: Living Will Declaration and Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care
advance_directive_requirements: A living will declaration must be signed by the declarant, or by another at the declarant's direction, and witnessed by two adult individuals, or signed in the presence of a notary public who notarizes it, under S.D. Codified Laws § 34-12D-2 as amended by 2023 Senate Bill 180.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse treatment, and a living will directs withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment when terminally ill and death is imminent or permanently unconscious. Hospice provides comfort care in place of aggressive, life-prolonging measures.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in South Dakota. S.D. Codified Laws § 22-16-37 makes it a Class 6 felony for a person to intentionally in any manner advise, encourage, abet, or assist another person in taking or attempting to take their own life.
notes: No medical aid in dying law has been adopted in South Dakota. Secondary sources conflict on whether South Dakota has a statewide POLST program, so no POLST URL is given.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Order for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: South Dakota also uses a Comfort One form for emergency care. A MOST does not replace an advance directive, and no official statewide POLST form URL was verified in this pass.

advance_directive_name: Advance Directive for Health Care
advance_directive_requirements: The form must be written and signed, and either notarized or witnessed by two competent adult witnesses. Neither witness may be the agent, and at least one witness must not be related to you by blood, marriage, or adoption and must not be entitled to any portion of your estate.
hospice_refusal: You may refuse life-prolonging treatment in an advance directive. Under Tenn. Code Ann. § 68-11-1814, death from withholding or withdrawing health care under the Tennessee Health Care Decisions Act is not suicide, euthanasia, homicide, or assisted suicide, and comfort care remains available.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Tennessee. Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-13-216 makes assisted suicide an offense, punishable as a Class D felony, when a person intentionally provides another person with the means to bring about their own death or participates in a physical act to do so.
notes: The Tennessee form combines the living will and medical power of attorney effective May 9, 2017. A state bar lawyer-referral URL was not verified with an exact official URL in this pass, so the official state health-care decision-making page is given as the help link.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment, form PH-4193)
polst_note: POST is a physician order for a terminally ill person that travels with the patient on transfer between facilities. It does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in the Advance Directive for Health Care, which combines the living will and medical power of attorney in one model form adopted by the Board for Licensing Health Care Facilities. advance_directive_name: Directive to Physicians and Family or Surrogates, and Medical Power of Attorney
advance_directive_requirements: Sign the directive in front of two adult witnesses, at least one of whom must be disinterested, or have it notarized, under the Texas Advance Directives Act, Tex. Health & Safety Code ch. 166.
hospice_refusal: You may direct withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment when you have a terminal or irreversible condition. Comfort care and pain relief must still be provided, and hospice is comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Texas. Tex. Penal Code § 22.08 makes it an offense, with intent to promote or assist suicide by another, to aid or attempt to aid the other to commit or attempt to commit suicide.
notes: The statutory Directive to Physicians form is in Tex. Health & Safety Code § 166.033. The State Bar LRIS offers up to a 30-minute consultation for no more than $20.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: Texas has no officially recognized statewide POLST form. A MOST is completed with a doctor and does not replace an advance directive, and Texas also has an Out-of-Hospital Do-Not-Resuscitate order under Tex. Health & Safety Code ch. 166.
proxy_how: Name an agent in a Medical Power of Attorney. The agent makes health care decisions, including decisions about life-prolonging care, when your doctor determines you can no longer make them.

advance_directive_name: Utah Advance Health Care Directive
hospice_refusal: Under Utah Code § 75-2a-102, an adult has the clear legal choice to accept or reject health care even if rejecting it will result in earlier death. Comfort care is always available, and hospice is comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Utah. Utah Code § 76-5-211 makes it a crime for a health care practitioner to knowingly provide medication or a procedure intended to cause death.
notes: The 2022 Utah End of Life Options Act (HB 74) failed in committee, so medical aid in dying remains unavailable. Witness/notary requirements for the directive were not verified from an official source in this pass, so that field is null. Utah Code Title 75, Chapter 2a was renumbered in 2024-2026, with advance directives now also appearing under Title 75A, Chapter 9.
polst_name: POLST (Provider Order for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: A POLST is a medical order on a form designated by the Department of Health and Human Services under Utah Code § 75-2a-106. It does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in Part I of the Utah Advance Health Care Directive. The agent makes health care decisions, including life-prolonging care, when your doctor determines you can no longer understand or communicate your preferences for health care.

advance_directive_name: Vermont Advance Directive for Health Care (Short Form and Long Form)
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be signed and witnessed as directed on the form. It is valid as soon as signing and witnessing is properly completed, and registering it with the Vermont Advance Directive Registry is optional and free.
hospice_refusal: You have the right to consent to or refuse any medical treatment. An advance directive guides care when you cannot speak for yourself, and comfort care and hospice remain available.
maid_eligibility: An adult 18 or older who is mentally capable, has an incurable terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less to live, and can self-administer the medication. The residency requirement was removed when H.190 was signed May 2, 2023.
maid_law: Patient Choice and Control at End of Life Act, 18 V.S.A. ch. 113, §§ 5281-5292 (Act 39, 2013)
maid_safeguards: Two physicians must confirm eligibility, informed decision, and voluntary request. The patient must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request on the required form. Only the patient can make the request, and the patient may change their mind at any time.
notes: Medical aid in dying cannot be requested through an advance directive or by a family member; the patient must be capable of deciding at the time. A Vermont Bar lawyer-referral phone number was not verified from an official page in this pass, so help_phone is null.
polst_name: DNR/COLST (Do Not Resuscitate Order / Clinician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: DNR/COLST is a clinician-signed medical order based on your current condition and goals. It is not an advance directive, and it travels with you so emergency responders can follow it.
proxy_how: Appoint an agent in Part 1 of the Advance Directive. The agent makes health care decisions for you when you cannot, following your instructions and values. You cannot appoint your doctor or other treating clinician as your agent.

advance_directive_name: Advance Medical Directive (Advance Directive)
hospice_refusal: You may direct withholding or withdrawal of life-prolonging procedures in an advance directive when you have a terminal condition. Comfort care and pain relief must still be provided, and a physician who finds proposed care medically or ethically inappropriate must document that finding and inform you or your agent.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Virginia. Va. Code § 54.1-2990(D) states that the Health Care Decisions Act shall not be construed to condone, authorize, or approve mercy killing or euthanasia or to permit any affirmative or deliberate act or omission to end life other than to permit the natural process of dying, and Va. Code § 8.01-622.1 provides an injunction against assisted suicide.
notes: The suggested advance directive form is in Va. Code § 54.1-2984, printed in full in the statute. The Virginia Lawyer Referral Service charges a $35 fee for a consultation of up to 30 minutes.
polst_name: POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: POST is a physician order recognized as a Durable Do Not Resuscitate order under 12VAC5-66. It must be signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant, and it accompanies the patient on transfer or discharge.

The agent makes health care decisions as specified in the directive when you are determined incapable of making an informed decision, including consenting to or refusing treatment, artificial respiration, artificially administered nutrition and hydration, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

advance_directive_name: Washington Advance Directive (Health Care Directive / Declaration, plus Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care)
hospice_refusal: You may refuse life-sustaining treatment in a Health Care Directive when terminally ill or permanently unconscious, under the Washington Natural Death Act, RCW 70.122. Hospice and palliative care focus on comfort.
maid_eligibility: A Washington resident adult 18 or older who is mentally competent, has a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less to live, and can self-administer the medication.
maid_law: Washington Death with Dignity Act, RCW 70.245 (Initiative 1000, effective March 5, 2009)
maid_safeguards: The patient must make oral and written requests, with a second oral request at least 15 days after the first, under RCW 70.245.090. Two physicians must confirm the diagnosis, prognosis, competence, and voluntary informed decision, and the patient may rescind the request at any time under RCW 70.245.100. A health care agent cannot request the medication for the patient.
notes: The Health Care Directive form is printed in full in RCW 70.122.030. The help phone is the WSBA CLEAR line for callers outside King County; it was not printed as a general referral number, so it is not listed.
polst_name: POLST (Portable Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: POLST is a portable physician order, implemented by the Department of Health and the Washington State Medical Association, summarizing wishes on resuscitation, medical interventions, antibiotics, and artificial feedings. It does not replace an advance directive.

advance_directive_name: West Virginia Combined Medical Power of Attorney and Living Will

In the November 2024 general election voters approved a constitutional amendment prohibiting any person or health care provider from participating in medically assisted suicide, euthanasia, or mercy killing, and W. Va. Code § 16-30-2 states it is not the intent of the Legislature to legalize, condone, authorize, or approve mercy killing or assisted suicide.
notes: West Virginia was the first state to enact a constitutional amendment prohibiting medical aid in dying. Witness and notary requirements for the combined form were not verified from an official source in this pass, so that field is null.

advance_directive_name: Declaration to Health Care Professionals (Wisconsin Living Will) and Power of Attorney for Health Care
advance_directive_requirements: Two witnesses are required. For the Power of Attorney for Health Care, witnesses must be at least 18, not related to you by blood, marriage, domestic partnership, or adoption, and not directly financially responsible for your health care.
hospice_refusal: You may refuse treatment and direct withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining procedures or feeding tubes in a Declaration when in a terminal condition or a persistent vegetative state. Pain relief and comfort care are not life-sustaining procedures, and hospice is comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Wisconsin. Wis. Stat. § 940.12 prohibits assisting suicide.
notes: Bills to authorize medical aid in dying (for example SB 739 in 2023 and SB 1013 / AB 1078 in 2021) were proposals only and did not become law. A State Bar Lawyer Referral phone number was not verified from an official page in this pass, so help_phone is null.

The Attorney General (OAG 10-14, 2014) concluded a POLST form does not carry the immunity of Wisconsin's statutory instruments, though it may be evidence of a person's health care wishes. Wisconsin uses a Do-Not-Resuscitate order under Wis. Stat. § 154.19.

advance_directive_name: Wyoming Advance Health Care Directive (Power of Attorney for Health Care and Instructions for Health Care)
advance_directive_requirements: Wyoming law allows an oral or written instruction and a written, signed health care power of attorney; there is no prescribed state form (the former statutory form was repealed in 2007).
hospice_refusal: You may refuse life-prolonging treatment in your Instructions for Health Care when you have an incurable, irreversible condition or are unconscious with no reasonable expectation of regaining consciousness. Comfort care is always provided, and hospice is comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Wyoming. Wyoming has no medical aid in dying law, and no statute specifically prohibiting physician-assisted suicide was verified from an official source in this pass.
notes: Wyoming repealed its former living-will declaration statute in 2005 and does not publish a current statutory advance directive form, so advance_directive_url and advance_directive_requirements are null. The governing law is the Wyoming Health Care Decisions Act, W.S. §§ 35-22-401 through 35-22-416, and WyoPOLST is under W.S. §§ 35-22-501 through 35-22-509. A Wyoming State Bar lawyer-referral URL and phone were not verified with an exact official URL in this pass.
polst_name: WyoPOLST (Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: WyoPOLST is a gold-paper medical order signed by a provider and the patient or representative, for seriously ill or frail patients. It is an addition to, not a replacement for, an advance directive, and Wyoming has no central POLST registry.
